extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers interested in Romantic-era poetic theory and the theory/practice of composing poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging lyrical/romantic poetry, especially regarding choice of subject, language register, and the roles of imagination and fancy. Emphasises how poetic effects are produced (sympathy, novelty, unity) and how imagination differs from mere memory or association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two cardinal aims of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry has two cardinal points: (1) the power of exciting the sympathy of the reader by a faithful adherence to the truth of nature, and (2) the power of giving the interest of novelty by the modifying colours of imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good poem should combine truthful depiction (to engage sympathy) with imaginative modification (to supply novelty). The author and Wordsworth pursued these complementary aims in the Lyrical Ballads: one focusing on supernatural interest, the other on everyday novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willing suspension of disbelief (poetic faith)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supernatural or romantic subjects must 'transfer from our inward nature a human interest and a semblance of truth sufficient to procure for these shadows of imagination that willing suspension of disbelief for the moment, which constitutes poetic faith.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make improbable or supernatural events effective in poetry, present them with human interest and dramatic truth so readers temporarily accept them. Failure to provide semblance of truth undermines poetic faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject selection for lyrical poetry (two-class model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two classes of subjects: (a) persons/characters supernatural or romantic, aiming to interest the affections by dramatic truth; (b) subjects from ordinary life, where novelty is produced by directing attention to the loveliness and wonders of the familiar world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether your poem will aim at the strange/marvellous (rendered believable by human truth) or at renewing the reader's perception of everyday life. The methods and diction appropriate to each differ accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ordinary language (language of real life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wordsworth proposed using 'the language of real life'—phrases and forms included in everyday speech—as a poetic register; the idea was to employ ordinary language to achieve sincerity and accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary language can produce pleasurable interest and authenticity, but beware of over-extending this prescription to all poetry; crude or meagre diction is not justified by the label of 'real life.' Match register to subject and intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poem vs prose: difference is combination and object
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem contains the same elements as a prose composition; the difference consists in a different combination of them, because a different object is proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing poetry, focus on how elements ( diction, image, rhythm, narrative) are recombined to pursue a poetic object (e.g., affect, synthesis, imaginative unity) rather than treating poetic language as categorically separate from prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary Imagination (creative, formative power)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary Imagination is 'the living power and prime agent of all human perception, and as a repetition in the finite mind of the eternal act of creation in the infinite I AM.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat primary imagination as the fundamental creative faculty: it is formative, vital, and the source of perception itself. Poetic creation should draw on this active, generative faculty rather than mere rearrangement of memories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary Imagination (recreative, unifying faculty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The secondary Imagination is an echo of the primary, 'co-existing with the conscious will, yet still as identical with the primary in the kind of its agency, and differing only in degree, and in the mode of its operation.' It 'dissolves, diffuses, dissipates, in order to recreate' and 'struggles to idealize and to unify.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In composition, secondary imagination is the poet's working faculty: it breaks down and reshapes material to create unified, idealized works. It is not mere fancy or associative play but an active, integrative process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fancy (associative memory, not creative synthesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fancy 'has no other counters to play with, but fixities and definites' and is 'no other than a mode of memory emancipated from the order of time and space.' Like ordinary memory, Fancy 'must receive all its materials ready made from the law of association.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate fancy from imagination when assessing poetic merit: fancy recombines existing images via association (useful for ornament), but lacks the dissolving-and-recreating power that produces true imaginative unity and originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justified use of technical terms and coinages
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical terms may be used when they 'tend to preclude confusion of thought' and assist memory by exclusive singleness of meaning; new-coined words are an evil only where unnecessary, but are justified when they accord with the end or final cause of language-use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specialized vocabulary when it clarifies subtle distinctions (e.g., imagination vs fancy). Avoid jargon that obscures; coin terms only when they serve conceptual precision and are defensible by utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match content to audience and prospectus (editorial prudence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers/authors should align content with the title/prospectus and audience expectation; including an abstruse metaphysical chapter in a volume announced as 'My Literary Life and Opinions' or as an introduction to poems risks alienating readers unprepared for such material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reader expectations, commercial effects, and fairness: reserve highly abstruse theoretical material for a specialized treatise rather than mixing it unexpectedly into a general literary volume. Anticipate complaints if content deviates from advertised scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception not limited to picturable imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of the modern creed that 'nothing is deemed a clear conception but what is representable by a distinct image'—this reduces the conceivable to the picturable and rejects continuous or infinite concepts simply because they lack a distinct image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing poetry, allow for abstract, continuous, or non-picturable conceptions that nevertheless have intellectual and emotional force. Clarity is not identical with picturability; avoid dismissing complex metaphysical or intuitive content merely because it resists concrete imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strive for unity and system in composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy (and by extension serious poetic composition) aims at 'unity and system'—intellectual parts should be distinguished for analysis but then restored to their unity in conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure poems achieve an internal coherence: separate elements analytically if needed, but compose toward a unified whole where parts cohere and reinforce the central imaginative object or effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative method via counteracting forces (constructive metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: A constructive imaginative method: conceive an indestructible power with two opposite and counteracting forces (centrifugal and centripetal) whose interpenetration generates finite forms; the product of two infinite counteracting forces must be a 'tertium aliquid' — a finite generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialectical or oppositional dynamics in imaginative construction (contraries that interpenetrate) to produce rich, finite poetic forms. This metaphysical metaphor suggests composing by holding and reconciling opposites rather than neutralizing them into mere rest.
